overview: Nvidia is in turmoil days after Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid allegations that he had extramarital affairs and was targeted by a Chinese spy. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is urging the company to hire an outsider, while tech figures including Elon Musk are calling for Huang's return, and investors are waiting on Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's stock market debut this week. In the US, flights were getting back to normal after Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop, which officials blamed on old equipment and a network failure; the administration is asking for $50 billion for air traffic control. Abroad, Iran attacked Bahrain for the second time in three days and Ukraine hit the bridge linking Russia and Crimea in a record drone barrage, ahead of a summit in Shenzhen this week where President Trump is set to meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

stories.headline: Flights return to normal after FAA ground stop as Trump officials seek $50 billion
stories.summary: Airline schedules were returning to normal Monday after Friday's nationwide ground stop, which officials linked to a failure in the air traffic control network. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said flights were nearing full capacity. President Trump, speaking about the outage for the first time, blamed the Biden administration, and his officials asked for $50 billion for air traffic control. The FAA is preparing to brief Congress.
stories.why_it_matters: The outage stranded tens of thousands of travelers just ahead of Thanksgiving week, and whether Congress funds a faster overhaul of the aging system affects how often this can happen again.
stories.background: The Federal Aviation Administration runs the system that keeps planes safely apart in U.S. airspace, and much of it relies on decades-old equipment and telecommunications lines. On Friday, Nov. 13, the FAA halted departures nationwide for more than four hours after a network failure, and airlines canceled thousands more flights over the weekend as they recovered. Smaller outages, including a September failure that hit Northeast airports, had already drawn attention to the system's fragility. Congress recently gave the Transportation Department $12.5 billion for upgrades, and the administration wants more.

facts.text: The FAA grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours on Friday, and disruptions lingered through the weekend.
According to FlightAware figures cited by NPR, nearly 25,000 flights were delayed and more than 9,000 canceled on Friday.
The FAA said airline schedules were returning to normal, and officials attributed the stop to aging infrastructure and legacy technology.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said U.S. flights were nearing full capacity on Monday.

Aviation experts and federal officials told the New York Times the outage began after a new piece of networking equipment flooded the rest of the system with data; the underlying cause is still unclear.
Officials said the outage was not related to the FAA's new $875 million AI-based forecasting system, called SMART, that is being rolled out.
In his first comments on the ground stop, Trump blamed the Biden administration for the FAA's problems.
Trump administration officials asked for $50 billion for air traffic control; Congress had recently provided $12.5 billion for upgrades.
CBS News reported that audits had for years flagged billions of dollars in non-competitive FAA contracts, delays and repeated technology breakdowns.
The FAA is preparing to brief Congress on the failure.

stories.headline: Van Hollen says he has a path to replace Schumer as Senate Democratic leader
stories.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Sunday that his bid to lead the incoming Democratic Senate majority instead of Chuck Schumer has a "wide-open" path and is gaining support. stories.background: Democrats won control of the Senate in this month's midterm elections, which would normally make their longtime leader, Chuck Schumer of New York, majority leader. Some Democrats, especially on the party's progressive wing, have been unhappy with Schumer's handling of fights with the Trump administration. Van Hollen, a Maryland senator, has emerged as his most prominent challenger, and Michigan's Elissa Slotkin has also been mentioned as a potential rival. stories.headline: Federal prosecutor warns Sen. Warren over planned probes of Trump allies
stories.summary: Aaron Reitz, a U.S. attorney in Texas, warned Sen. Elizabeth Warren on Sunday of possible legal consequences over her plans to investigate President Trump and his associates. stories.background: Democrats won majorities in Congress in this month's midterms, which will give them control of committees and the power to launch investigations of the Trump administration starting in January. Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, has said she plans to investigate people close to the president. stories.headline: Judge halts Trump's plan to close a historic D.C. public golf course
stories.summary: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes on Saturday ordered a two-week pause on any work at East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, blocking its planned Sunday closure for a 15-month renovation. stories.why_it_matters: The case tests how much control a president has over public land in the capital, and the course is Washington's most popular public golf facility.
stories.background: East Potomac Golf Links is a public course on federal parkland near the White House. The Trump administration wants to turn it into a championship-level course, and opponents sued, arguing the project bypasses legal requirements. In October, Reyes issued an injunction barring further tree removal and requiring advance notice before any closure, and the administration appealed to the D.C. Circuit. The administration had planned to close the course on Sunday.

stories.headline: NTSB says tanker's steering failed before it hit a New Orleans cruise ship
stories.summary: A preliminary NTSB finding says the tanker Atlantic Asphalt suffered a steering failure that kept its rudder stuck before it crashed into the docked cruise ship American Heritage in New Orleans on Friday. Investigators recovered audio of warning whistles and emergency orders. The Port of New Orleans is suing the tanker's owners for at least $1 million.
stories.why_it_matters: The finding points investigators toward an equipment failure on a busy commercial river that passenger vessels share with large cargo ships.
stories.background: On Friday, the tanker Atlantic Asphalt struck the American Heritage riverboat-style cruise ship while it was docked on the Mississippi River in New Orleans, capsizing it. Passengers, crew and two police officers ended up in the water, but no one was killed, leading to the nickname "miracle on the Mississippi." The National Transportation Safety Board investigates major transport accidents and typically takes a year or more to issue a final cause.

The tanker's voyage recorder captured warning whistles and emergency orders before the collision.
The Port of New Orleans is seeking at least $1 million in damages from the tanker's owners; no one was killed.

stories.headline: Iran targets a US base in Bahrain for the second time in three days
stories.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it sent six drones at the radar of a US air defense site at Bahrain's Riffa base on Sunday, its second attack on Bahrain in three days. After a lull of roughly two months, the US carried out limited strikes on Iran's Qeshm island in recent weeks, and Iran describes its new attacks as retaliation. Washington and Tehran have been holding peace talks that have not produced a deal.

stories.headline: Ukraine hits the Crimean Bridge in its largest drone barrage of the war
stories.summary: Ukraine launched more than 1,300 drones at Russia overnight, aiming toward Moscow and hitting the bridge that links Russia to occupied Crimea. The Kremlin called the damage minor, while Crimea's Russian-installed governor said traffic over the bridge was limited. The strike came a day after President Zelenskyy said US-controlled limits on Starshield satellite terminals were letting Russian attacks on Ukraine's power grid get through.
stories.why_it_matters: The war is escalating on both sides heading into winter, when Russian strikes on Ukraine's power and rail networks hit civilians hardest; the attack also lands days before Trump meets Putin and Xi.
stories.background: Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 and built the Kerch Strait bridge to connect it to Russian territory; Ukraine has struck it before because it is a key supply route. Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, and both sides now rely heavily on long-range drones. Ukraine uses SpaceX's Starlink and its military version, Starshield, to guide drones, including interceptor drones that shoot down Russian attack drones. Kyiv has said for weeks that speed limits on those terminals stop its fast interceptors from working. US-brokered peace talks recently ended without a breakthrough.

Crimea's Russian-backed governor, Sergei Aksyonov, said the strike limited traffic over the bridge.
Bloomberg reported the barrage likely also hit an oil refinery and came after US-brokered peace talks ended without a breakthrough.
The Kyiv Independent reported Moscow Oblast was among the main targets and that a fuel depot in Azov, Russia, was reportedly on fire after drone attacks.
Zelenskyy said Russia struck energy and railway infrastructure in eight regions on Saturday night and that many strikes got through because of limits on Starshield terminals.
Zelenskyy said in October that Starlink speed restrictions had hindered the interception of jet-powered Shahed drones, and that about 2,000 Bars interceptor drones were grounded by the caps.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas called Russia's demands in the peace talks 'absurd' and said a ceasefire must come first.

stories.headline: China confirms the first Xi-Trump-Putin summit, set for Thursday in Shenzhen
stories.summary: China's foreign ministry confirmed that Xi Jinping will host Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on Thursday, Nov. 19, the first meeting of the three leaders. Beijing gave no agenda but said the meeting has 'groundbreaking significance'. US officials have pointed to the war in Ukraine, the Middle East and nuclear arms control as likely topics.
stories.why_it_matters: The leaders of the three largest military powers will discuss wars that drive energy prices and nuclear risk. In the day's feed the story was covered by center and left-leaning outlets only.
stories.background: The meeting is planned around the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which China is hosting in Shenzhen this week. Earlier in November Beijing said only that it was in talks about a possible three-way meeting. The US is at war with Iran, a partner of both China and Russia, and is trying to broker an end to Russia's war in Ukraine. Trump is also locked in trade disputes with China and others.

The fighting is tied to the wider regional war that the US and Israel launched against Iran in February, and the Houthis have also attacked Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping.

stories.headline: Huge crowd rallies in Prague against government plan for public broadcasters
stories.summary: A very large crowd gathered in Prague's Letná Park on Sunday to oppose Prime Minister Andrej Babiš's plan to replace license fees for Czech Television and Czech Radio with direct state funding. Most reports put turnout in the hundreds of thousands, and organizers said it beat a March protest of more than 200,000. Critics say the change would threaten the broadcasters' independence.
stories.why_it_matters: How public media are paid for decides how easily a government can squeeze them, and Czech voters are pushing back on a pattern seen elsewhere in central Europe.
stories.background: Babiš, a billionaire, returned as prime minister at the head of a nationalist-leaning coalition. His government wants to scrap the fees households pay for public TV and radio and fund the broadcasters from the state budget instead. Opponents, including the broadcasters' staff, see this as a way to gain leverage over newsrooms, and the plan has drawn repeated protests this year, including rallies in Prague's Old Town Square in October. Letná Park is where huge crowds gathered during the 1989 Velvet Revolution that ended communist rule.

stories.headline: Nearly 2,200 migrants reach Spain's Canary Islands in two days
stories.summary: Spain's maritime rescue service said nearly 2,200 migrants reached the Canary Islands by boat over the weekend, mostly from West Africa, continuing a surge that led to a migration emergency declaration earlier in the week. Islands officials say they are struggling to cope. Separately, five EU countries were expected on Monday to announce a deportation center for rejected asylum seekers in Rwanda.

stories.background: The Canary Islands are Spanish territory off northwest Africa, and people from Senegal, Gambia, Guinea and nearby countries try to reach them in overcrowded wooden boats. Arrivals rose sharply in early November, especially on the small island of El Hierro, which declared an emergency. Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta also recently faced a migration crisis. The EU tightened its migration rules in late 2025, opening the way for 'return hubs' outside the bloc.

stories.headline: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if US trade talks fail
stories.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada could work with Chinese carmakers if negotiations with President Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry. He said any Chinese investment would have to bring real manufacturing to Canada, not just assembly of imported parts. A day earlier he said he was making progress with Trump on a trade deal.

stories.background: The US and Canada have been in a months-long tariff fight since Trump imposed duties on Canadian goods, including cars and parts. North American carmaking is deeply integrated, with parts crossing the border many times. Carney, a former central banker who became prime minister in 2025, has sought new trade ties in Europe and Asia. He is in Asia for regional summits, including APEC in China, where Xi, Putin and Trump are also due.

stories.headline: Tech stocks slide into a week set by Nvidia earnings and Anthropic's IPO
stories.summary: A selloff in technology shares carried into Monday, with U.S. stock futures and emerging-market stocks falling as investors waited on two events: Nvidia's quarterly results on Tuesday and the pricing of Anthropic's initial public offering, expected Wednesday with trading to start Thursday. Weakness in Asian AI stocks overnight added to the pressure, according to The Wall Street Journal.
stories.why_it_matters: A handful of AI companies now make up a large share of the stock indexes held in most 401(k)s and index funds, so how this week goes for Nvidia and Anthropic can move ordinary retirement balances.
stories.background: Since 2023, investor enthusiasm for artificial intelligence has driven much of the stock market's gains, led by chipmaker Nvidia, the world's most valuable company by market value. Nvidia's shares have fallen sharply in recent weeks amid a leadership crisis tied to questions about chip sales reaching China. At the same time, Anthropic, the AI lab that makes the Claude models, is preparing one of the largest stock offerings on record. The Nasdaq Composite ended last week down nearly 6% over the past month, while the Dow, which is less tech-heavy, was up over the same period.

Nvidia is scheduled to report earnings on Tuesday.

stories.summary: U.S. Treasury yields dipped Monday after jumping last week on hotter inflation data and hawkish comments from Federal Reserve officials, the WSJ reported. Its next meeting is in December, and markets are now debating the size of a hike rather than whether one comes.

stories.summary: Japan's economy contracted at an annualized 0.1% in July-September, its first contraction in a year, according to official data reported by Reuters and the Financial Times. stories.why_it_matters: Japan is the world's fourth-largest economy and a major U.S. trading partner; its slowdown is another sign of how the oil shock from the Iran war is weighing on households worldwide.
stories.background: Japan imports nearly all its oil, so the jump in energy prices since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has hit its households hard. The government had subsidized household energy bills, but those subsidies reportedly ended in September. The Bank of Japan has been slowly raising interest rates after decades near zero, and weak growth makes further increases harder to justify. On Monday, BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda told a government panel that wage growth is 'quite strong.'

stories.headline: Diesel drops below $6 a gallon, easing a key inflation pressure
stories.summary: U.S. retail diesel prices fell below $6 a gallon for the first time since early September, Bloomberg reported, a two-month low driven by easing geopolitical tensions and weaker demand. Goldman Sachs separately forecast a 'sizable' oil surplus next year that it expects to pull prices lower.
stories.why_it_matters: Diesel moves the trucks and farm equipment behind most goods, so cheaper diesel can eventually ease food and shipping costs that have pushed prices up this fall.
stories.background: Diesel prices surged this year as the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran disrupted oil supplies and Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries cut fuel output. Because diesel feeds into transport and farming costs, its price has helped push up food and energy inflation. Brent crude, the global benchmark, was around $92 a barrel last week, down about 29% over a month.

facts.text: Retail diesel fell below $6 a gallon for the first time since early September.
The New York Post attributed the decline to easing tensions and weaker demand.

Goldman Sachs expects Brent to average $88 a barrel next year and ease to $78 by the end of 2027, citing a sizable supply surplus.

stories.headline: Tech failure halts specialized high school exam, sending students home
stories.summary: Many students taking the Specialized High School Admissions Test on Saturday could not get into or finish the online exam because of what city officials called a technical problem on the testing vendor's platform, and some were sent home early. The Education Department said students who could not finish will be rescheduled automatically. The department did not give a cause beyond the vendor problem in the initial reports.
stories.why_it_matters: For eighth graders aiming at Stuyvesant, Bronx Science and the other test-in schools, this single exam decides admission. Families now have to plan for a retake and wait for the city to explain what went wrong.
stories.background: The SHSAT is the only thing that decides admission to eight of the city's nine specialized high schools, including Stuyvesant. Eighth graders take it each fall. In 2025 the city moved the exam to a digital format, and Chalkbeat reported then that the first computer-based test went mostly smoothly, with only a handful of students rescheduled. The city's Education Department oversees the test, which an outside vendor delivers online.

stories.headline: Flatbush holds vigil for eight killed in building collapse
stories.summary: Neighbors, firefighters and elected officials gathered in Flatbush on Sunday to remember the eight people killed when an apartment building collapsed on Nov. 11, amNY reported. The collapse also injured 18 people. City building inspectors have been examining the site, which was next to an excavation, and no official cause had been announced in the reports found.
stories.why_it_matters: Eight deaths make this a major disaster for the neighborhood, and the inspectors' findings on the neighboring excavation will matter to anyone living next to a construction site. Survivors are still dealing with what they lost.
stories.background: On the afternoon of Nov. 11 a three-story building in Flatbush, Brooklyn, fell into a neighboring open construction site where excavation was under way, according to wire reports. Firefighters dug through the rubble for survivors; early reports that day counted one death, and the toll later reached eight. The city Department of Buildings sent inspectors to assess the site and check nearby structures. Coverage since has turned to survivors and rescuers.

stories.headline: NYPD fatally shoots suspected kidnapper on the Belt Parkway
stories.summary: Police shot and killed a man on Brooklyn's Belt Parkway on Saturday night after a report that a woman was trying to get out of his van. Police said he rammed police and civilian vehicles while trying to get away. The woman inside the van was not hurt, and police said the man had a history of domestic violence cases involving her.

Officers tried to stop the driver on the Belt Parkway, and police say he used the van to ram cars to escape before officers opened fire. stories.headline: Amazon and Urban League threaten to sue over Mamdani-backed delivery bill
stories.summary: Amazon and the National Urban League have threatened to sue the city if the City Council passes the Delivery Protection Act, City & State reported. Mayor Mamdani supports the bill, which would end the use of third-party contractors for last-mile delivery. The bill still needs a Council vote, which the speaker has not scheduled.
stories.why_it_matters: The bill would change how most packages reach New York doorsteps and who employs the drivers. Supporters say it protects workers; Amazon says it could make deliveries slower and more expensive.
stories.background: Council Member Tiffany Cabán's bill would make companies that run last-mile delivery hubs in the city get a license and hire delivery drivers directly. That would end Amazon's model of contracting with independent delivery companies. The Council heard the bill in committee in April 2026, and Mamdani endorsed it in August. Unions have pushed Council Speaker Menin to bring it to a vote. Amazon has warned it could reconsider where it runs distribution facilities.

stories.headline: THE CITY maps the odds and price tags of NYC's housing lottery
stories.summary: THE CITY published a set of explainers on Monday about the city's affordable housing lottery: how area median income sets rents, how to apply, and the odds of winning. Its odds estimate is based on the city housing agency's lottery outcome data from January 2022 through October 2024. The package also points out that some so-called affordable units rent for thousands of dollars a month.
stories.why_it_matters: The lottery is the main way New Yorkers can get a new below-market apartment. Knowing how incomes are matched to units, and how long the odds are, helps applicants decide which listings are worth trying for.
stories.background: New York City fills new subsidized apartments through a lottery run on the Housing Connect website by the Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD). Rents and eligibility are tied to area median income, which is why, as THE CITY notes, some 'affordable' units are far from cheap. A 2019 city law, Local Law 217, requires HPD to publish data on applications and signed leases. THE CITY used that data in 2020 to report that the lowest-income applicants faced the worst odds.

facts.text: Recent lottery listings included a Murray Hill two-bedroom at $4,518 a month and a Flatbush studio at $2,022, THE CITY reported.
THE CITY estimated lottery odds from HPD's Local Law 217 report, covering Jan. 1, 2022, through Oct. 31, 2024, and more than 10.9 million entries.
Citing the city's 2023 Housing and Vacancy Survey, THE CITY said 18% of renters spend 30% to 50% of their income on housing.
Local Law 217 requires HPD to report lottery applications and signed leases broken down by income, race and borough.
THE CITY's 2020 analysis found the poorest applicants faced the longest odds.

concept.explanation: GDP is the total value of everything a country produces in a given period, and it is the main yardstick for whether an economy is growing or shrinking. It rises when households spend more, businesses invest, governments buy more and exports beat imports, and it falls when those weaken, as in Japan, where high energy prices squeezed shoppers and the economy shrank in July to September. Figures are often 'annualized', meaning a quarter's change is scaled up to show what it would be over a full year. GDP reaches your wallet through jobs and pay: a growing economy usually means more hiring and raises, while two quarters of decline in a row are commonly called a recession, when layoffs tend to rise and central banks may cut interest rates.
